title: US Economy Sheds 23,000 Jobs in July as Hiring Stalls Unexpectedly
excerpt: Nonfarm payrolls posted a surprise decline while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, driven by workers leaving the labor force rather than finding jobs.
body:
• Nonfarm payrolls fell 23,000 in July, far below the 80,000 gain economists had forecast, with prior months revised sharply lower
  • The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%, but only because 264,000 people dropped out of the labor force, pushing participation to a five-year low
  • Average hourly earnings rose 3.2% year-over-year to $37.62, still trailing the 3.5% annual pace of consumer price increases
  • Markets rallied as traders slashed odds of a September Fed rate hike to roughly 20%, down from 55% before the report

The U.S. economy unexpectedly shed 23,000 jobs in July, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, delivering a sharp miss against the 80,000 gain economists polled by Reuters had forecast and raising fresh questions about whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month.

The headline number was ugly enough on its own. But the revisions told a worse story: the BLS cut its estimates for May and June by a combined 103,000 jobs. June payrolls were slashed to just 20,000 from an initially reported 57,000, while May was revised down to 63,000. The pattern points to a labor market that has been weaker than the data suggested in real time.

A Misleading Unemployment Drop

The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2% in June, but the decline offered little comfort. It was driven not by a surge in hiring but by 264,000 people exiting the labor force entirely. The labor force participation rate slid to 61.4%, the lowest reading since February 2021.

"With job opportunities remaining scarce, more workers are exiting the labor market entirely."

— Nicole Bachaud, Labor Economist, ZipRecruiter

The numbers come after a period of slowing momentum. Job growth decelerated through the spring and summer, with payrolls averaging 111,000 per month over the second quarter before tipping negative in July. While seasonal adjustment quirks tend to soften July readings, the scale of the miss and the downward revisions suggest more than a statistical artifact.

Wages Lag Inflation

Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 2 cents to $37.62 in July, translating to a 3.2% year-over-year gain. That trails the 3.5% annual increase in consumer prices recorded in June. The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index for July, due August 12, will show whether the squeeze on real wages continued.

The report lands in an economy navigating multiple crosscurrents. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, now in its sixth month, has pushed oil prices higher and clouded the outlook for both inflation and growth. Domestic demand grew at its fastest pace in more than three years in the second quarter, but the ISM services employment index contracted in July, foreshadowing the soft payrolls print.

Markets Price Out a September Hike

Wall Street responded with a relief rally. The S&P 500 gained 0.25% to 7,728.83 in early trading, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.69% to 26,530.07 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 55 points. Collaboration software maker Atlassian jumped 34.5% and chipmaker Microchip Technology advanced 11.4% after both forecast quarterly revenue above estimates.

In the bond market, the 2-year Treasury yield fell 8 basis points to 4.16% and the 10-year note dropped 6 basis points to 4.61%. The U.S. dollar index slipped 0.5% to 99.43.

"Even with a negative job print, the job market remains healthy. But it gives the Fed some room to pause in September."

— Anthony Saglimbene, Chief Market Strategist, Ameriprise Financial

Money market data showed traders pared back expectations for a September rate increase to about 20%, down from 55% before the report, according to LSEG data. The Fed, under Chair Kevin Warsh, left its benchmark overnight rate in the 3.50%-3.75% range last week. Three members of the policy-setting committee dissented, preferring a quarter-point hike.

What Comes Next

The central question is whether July marks a temporary summer soft patch or the beginning of a more sustained deterioration. Layoffs remain low — planned job cuts by U.S. employers dropped 27% in July to the lowest level since July 2024, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. But the combination of negative payroll growth, collapsing participation, and persistent downward revisions suggests the labor market is weaker than the headline unemployment rate implies.

The Fed has offered investors little forward guidance under Warsh, putting the focus squarely on incoming data. The August jobs report, due September 5, and the July CPI print on August 12 will be decisive for whether a rate hike returns to the table.
nri_angle: July jobs data shapes the employment outlook and Fed rate path affecting millions of workers across the U.S. economy.
